question: Can a corpus of real-world neural network architectures, scraped from public model hubs and normalized to parameter-free ONNX-operator DAGs, supply enough prior knowledge to support automated architecture generation without a predefined search space (the authors' 'AIGNNA' goal), and can the same corpus double as a benchmark for graph neural networks?

key_findings.claim: The dataset pipeline turns 174K retrieved real-world models into 7,629 unique operator-level architecture DAGs covering 184 of 193 ONNX operator types, roughly 12.6M nodes and 16.1M edges, across 31 task types, with parameters stripped for privacy.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3 describes the four-stage pipeline (hub retrieval, ONNX conversion via optimum/tf2onnx/PyTorch export, DAG extraction into NetworkX with operator attributes and data-flow order, Weisfeiler-Lehman hash deduplication). Table 3 gives the funnel: 743.5K retrievable, 341K ONNX-convertible, 174K converted, 7,629 after isomorphism filtering. The datasheet states 12.6M nodes, 16.1M edges, and 184 supported operator types.

key_findings.claim: The authors read the sub-1% architectural-uniqueness rate as evidence that current manual and NAS design methods produce little architectural innovation, but this inference depends entirely on the WL-hash identity notion.
key_findings.evidence: Page 5 argues that fewer than 1% of processed models are architecturally heterogeneous and concludes existing design methods 'have a limited impact on architectural innovation.' The WL hash iterates over operator types and attributes, so the uniqueness count is sensitive to whether attribute-only variants count as distinct; the paper publishes separate 'w/ attributes' and 'w/o attributes' filter series precisely because the two notions give different corpora, yet the innovation claim is stated without that qualification.

key_findings.claim: In the local paradigm, data-flow design (edge existence prediction) is nearly saturated while operator design (node-type prediction) collapses on the long-tail operator distribution.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4: GCN reaches AUC 0.9922/0.9938 and AP 0.9913/0.9929 with/without attributes on link prediction. Table 5: despite accuracies of 0.71-0.93, the best F1 for operator classification is 0.3646 (SAGE, w/o attributes) and GAE falls to F1 0.0537 with attributes; GAT runs out of memory with attributes. The authors attribute the gap to many infrequent operator types, and the t-SNE audit shows models separating only the top-500 frequent operators.

key_findings.claim: The global paradigm is only nominally validated: a single DiGress run on architectures capped at 300 nodes reports a test negative log-likelihood of 'at least 345.4988' with no baseline, sample-quality metric, or validity check of generated architectures.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5.2.2 is one short paragraph. It states compute restrictions forced training on graphs with 1-300 nodes (the corpus reaches hundreds of thousands of nodes), reports only the NLL number, and defers everything else to future work. No generated architecture is shown, executed, or evaluated for well-formedness, so from-scratch generation feasibility is asserted rather than demonstrated.

key_findings.claim: Main-text and appendix result tables disagree for the same experiments without explanation.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 (main text) reports GCN link-prediction AUC 0.9922 (w/ attributes) and SAGE 0.9169, while appendix Table 8 reports 0.9933 and 0.9702 for the same configuration names; operator-design Tables 5 and 11 likewise differ (e.g., GCN accuracy 0.8684 vs 0.7454 w/ attributes). The appendix describes seeds and hyperparameters but never reconciles the two sets, and the checklist marks error bars N/A, so run-to-run variance is unquantified.

key_findings.claim: Younger carries no performance labels, so generation objectives cannot be scored against task quality; this is the core structural difference from NAS benchmarks and the main obstacle to the AIGNNA program.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 contrasts Younger with NAS-Bench-style datasets but omits that those datasets attach trained accuracies to every architecture while Younger attaches none. The author-contribution note records that performance-metric annotations were considered and 'Younger did not include this.' Consequently the paper's own experiments can only measure structural reconstruction (AUC/F1/NLL), never whether a designed architecture is good.

key_findings.claim: The operator-design task rests on community detection as a building-block extractor, which the authors themselves state has no supporting evidence.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D.2.1 applies Clauset-Newman-Moore modularity maximization to each DAG, labels community boundary nodes as prediction targets, and deduplicates subgraphs (38,803 w/ attributes; 29,581 w/o). The text concedes 'there is no evidence to suggest that the subgraphs extracted by community detection are effective building blocks for neural network architecture,' so the benchmark's node-classification difficulty may reflect an arbitrary subgraph notion rather than architectural structure.

anchors.section: Appendix D.2.1, boundary definition and caveat

key_findings.claim: As a GNN benchmark, Younger occupies a distinct regime: few graphs (7,629) that are individually large (mean ~1,658 nodes, ~2,113 edges) with 184 node types, unlike citation networks (one huge graph) or molecule sets (many tiny graphs).
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 compares Cora/CiteSeer/PubMed (single graphs), ZINC/QM9 (tens of thousands of ~20-node graphs, 5-10 node types) with Younger. Graph-embedding t-SNE shows variants of the same architecture family (e.g., RoBERTa and ViT, both Transformer-based) clustering together, indicating the corpus contains many variants per family.

anchors.section: Table 2 and 2.2 Benchmarking Graph Neural Network

method.core_idea: Build architectural prior knowledge by scraping real deployed models from four public hubs, normalizing them to the ONNX operator set, stripping parameters, and representing each model as an attributed operator-level DAG; then pose architecture design as learning problems over this corpus at two granularities (local component refinement and global from-scratch generation) and reuse the corpus as a structurally unusual GNN benchmark.
method.mechanism: Automated tools pull models from Hugging Face Hub, ONNX Model Zoo, PyTorch Hub, and Kaggle Models; optimum, tf2onnx, and the PyTorch exporter convert them to ONNX (~2000+ PyTorch operators map onto ~193 standard ONNX operators); a custom extractor rewrites each ONNX protobuf into a NetworkX DAG whose nodes record operator type plus attribute configuration and whose edges record ordered data flow; Weisfeiler-Lehman graph hashing over node operator information removes isomorphic architectures (174K models -> 7,629 DAGs). Local paradigm experiments treat graphs as homogeneous: data-flow design is link prediction with negative edge sampling on an 8:1:1 architecture split, and operator design is node classification of community-boundary operators over CNM-detected subgraphs, each under two feature configurations (operator type only vs type+attributes). Global paradigm trains the DiGress discrete graph-diffusion model on architectures with at most 300 nodes and reports test NLL.
assumptions: ONNX conversion preserves the architectural semantics of models built in different frameworks, and the ~53% of models that fail conversion do not bias the corpus in ways that matter.
WL hashing over operator types and attributes is the right identity notion for 'the same architecture', so the 7,629-count and the sub-1% uniqueness claim are meaningful.
Treating operator DAGs as homogeneous graphs (one node type) is an adequate first evaluation regime despite operators having heterogeneous attribute schemas.
Community detection by modularity maximization yields subgraphs that behave like architectural building blocks for the operator-design task.
Architecture topology alone, without weights or performance labels, encodes enough prior knowledge to eventually support generation of useful new architectures.
Log-likelihood of a graph diffusion model is an informative first signal of from-scratch generation feasibility.

techniques.role: Maps models from heterogeneous frameworks onto a shared ~193-operator vocabulary, collapsing framework-specific operator sets and enabling cross-hub comparison.
Rewrites ONNX protobuf models into NetworkX DAGs recording operator type, attribute configuration, and ordered data-flow edges while discarding weights for privacy and safety.
Hashes each DAG over node operator information so isomorphic architectures collapse to one entry, defining the corpus's uniqueness notion.
Clauset-Newman-Moore modularity maximization carves each architecture into candidate building blocks whose boundary nodes become operator-prediction targets.
Casts data-flow design as edge-existence classification with sampled non-edges, evaluated by AUC/F1/AP.
Casts operator design as multi-class prediction over up to tens of thousands of operator-attribute classes, exposing extreme class imbalance.
Uses DiGress as the global-paradigm baseline to generate whole architecture DAGs from noise, size-capped at 300 nodes.
Visualizes node, subgraph, and graph embeddings to diagnose long-tail operator imbalance and confirm that architecture-family variants cluster.

evaluations.setting: Data-flow design (link prediction) on the filtered corpus, 8:1:1 split (5,994/690/685 architectures w/ attributes; 5,612/639/648 w/o), homogeneous node features
evaluations.result: GCN best: AUC 0.9922 / AP 0.9913 (w/ attributes) and AUC 0.9938 / AP 0.9929 (w/o); GAT best F1 0.8079; appendix rerun (Table 8) shifts numbers (GCN AUC 0.9933/0.9949, SAGE AUC 0.9702 w/ attributes) without explanation.
evaluations.baseline: GCN vs GAT vs GraphSAGE against each other; no non-GNN heuristic or prior-work baseline

evaluations.setting: Operator design (node classification of community-boundary operators) over 38,803 (w/ attr) / 29,581 (w/o attr) deduplicated subgraphs, 8:1:1 split
evaluations.result: Best F1 0.3646 at accuracy 0.9250 (SAGE w/o attributes); with attributes all F1 <= 0.21 and GAT is OOM; accuracy-F1 gap shows majority-class bias from long-tail operators.
evaluations.baseline: GCN, GAT, GAE, VGAE, GraphSAGE against each other

evaluations.setting: Global paradigm: DiGress trained on architectures with node counts in [1,300] due to compute limits
evaluations.result: NLL of at least 345.4988; no samples shown, no validity/uniqueness/novelty metrics, no downstream evaluation of generated architectures.

evaluations.setting: Corpus statistics vs existing graph benchmarks
evaluations.metric: Graph/node/edge counts, node-type diversity, operator frequency distribution
evaluations.result: 7,629 graphs averaging ~1,658 nodes / ~2,113 edges with 184 node types, spanning a dozen to hundreds of thousands of nodes; top-30 operator histogram and t-SNE plots document a heavy long tail.
evaluations.baseline: Cora/CiteSeer/PubMed, ZINC, QM9 (Table 2); NAS-Bench-101/201/NLP/ASR and DeepNets-1M (Table 1)

limitations: Author-stated (p.7): all experiments treat architectures as homogeneous graphs; heterogeneous treatment of operator types/attributes is left to future work.

Author-stated (p.14): only ~341K of 743.5K retrievable models are ONNX-convertible, so the corpus covers part of the real-world space; representativeness is asserted via coverage of mainstream architectures, not validated.
Author-stated (p.9): compute restrictions capped global-paradigm training at 300-node graphs, while the corpus contains graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes.
Author-stated (p.31, checklist): no error bars or multi-seed replication for any experiment.
Author-stated (p.23): no evidence that community-detection subgraphs are effective architectural building blocks.

Reviewer-identified: no performance, latency, or trainability labels accompany any architecture, so neither the local nor the global paradigm can be evaluated on whether designed architectures are actually good; the paper's own contribution note confirms performance annotations were excluded.
Reviewer-identified: main-text and appendix tables report different numbers for identically described experiments (e.g., GCN AUC 0.9922 vs 0.9933), and neither set is identified as canonical.

Reviewer-identified: the sub-1% uniqueness and 'limited architectural innovation' claim inherits the WL-hash equivalence choice; attribute-only variants and near-duplicates are not analyzed under alternative equivalences.
Reviewer-identified: the DiGress NLL is uninterpretable without a baseline or validity metric; feasibility of from-scratch generation is not demonstrated.

Reviewer-identified: hub composition is dominated by Hugging Face (143.5K of 159.5K retrieved), so task and family coverage likely skews toward Transformer-era NLP models; no per-family composition table is given.

Reviewer-identified: the CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license forbids derivative redistribution, which constrains the community-extension workflow the paper itself advocates, and upstream model-license conflicts are handled only by takedown on request.
failure_modes: Long-tail operator frequency makes learned models collapse onto majority operators; macro F1 stays below 0.37 even for the best baseline, so operator-level design assistance is unreliable off the head of the distribution.
Expanding node features to operator-attribute combinations explodes the class space, causing GAT out-of-memory failures and degrading every model's F1.

Architectures with very large node counts (up to hundreds of thousands) exceed both generation-model capacity and GNN memory, so exactly the most complex real-world architectures are the least served.

Conversion-failure bias: models that cannot be exported to ONNX (custom ops, dynamic control flow) are silently absent, which will exclude many novel research architectures the dataset is meant to inspire.
A generator trained only on topology can emit DAGs that are syntactically valid graphs but not executable networks (shape mismatches, dangling inputs); no validity checker exists in the release.

WL-hash deduplication keyed on attributes can either inflate uniqueness (trivially different hyperparameters counted as new architectures) or, keyed without attributes, merge genuinely different designs, destabilizing corpus statistics between filter series.
reusable_insights: Normalizing multi-framework models to a compact operator IR (ONNX) is a practical route to corpus-scale architecture mining: ~2000+ framework operators reduce to ~193.
Parameter stripping decouples architecture sharing from weight privacy/IP concerns, enabling owners to contribute designs without leaking models.

WL graph hashing gives a cheap, deterministic architecture-identity notion for deduplication at 100K+ model scale; the equivalence choice (with vs without attributes) should always be published as separate corpus variants.

Structural-reconstruction tasks split sharply by type: edge-existence prediction over real architecture DAGs is nearly saturated, while long-tail node-type prediction remains open - useful when designing benchmarks that should not saturate.
A corpus of few-but-large attributed DAGs (10^3 graphs x 10^3 nodes x ~184 node types) stresses GNN scalability and imbalance handling in a regime citation and molecule benchmarks do not cover.

Dataset value for generation depends on labels for the generation objective; topology-only corpora support imitation of existing designs but not optimization toward quality, a gap any AIGNNA follow-up must close.
open_questions: Can performance, latency, or trainability labels be attached to Younger architectures (measured or predicted) so that generation can be steered and scored, closing the gap with NAS benchmarks?
What fraction of DiGress-generated operator DAGs are executable networks, and what validity metric should replace or accompany NLL for architecture generation?
How do the local-paradigm results change under heterogeneous-graph treatment, where each operator type has its own attribute schema?
Why do the main-text and appendix tables disagree, and what is the seed-to-seed variance of every reported metric?
Does the sub-1% uniqueness figure survive alternative architecture equivalences (ignoring attribute-only differences, collapsing repeated blocks, canonicalizing widths/depths)?
Can conditioning signals (task type, parameter budget, hub provenance) steer global generation the way predictor guidance steers DiffusionNAG inside fixed search spaces?
Is community detection replaceable by motif mining or repeated-subgraph detection that provably recovers human-designed blocks (residual units, attention heads)?

competitive_landscape.title: NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
competitive_landscape.relationship: Cited predecessor benchmark and the design point Younger argues against
competitive_landscape.difference: NAS-Bench-101 exhaustively trains 423K cell architectures inside one fixed macro-architecture on CIFAR-10 and attaches accuracy labels to every entry, enabling reproducible search evaluation; Younger removes the macro-architecture restriction and spans 193 operator types and 31 tasks from real deployed models, but provides no trained-performance labels, so search/generation quality cannot be scored against it.

competitive_landscape.title: Parameter Prediction for Unseen Deep Architectures
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepNets-1M contains one million synthetically generated computational graphs (about 15 primitive types, image classification only) built to train a graph hypernetwork that predicts parameters for unseen networks; Younger instead harvests 174K real-world models into 7,629 deduplicated operator-level DAGs across 30+ tasks and targets architecture generation rather than parameter prediction, with no hypernetwork or downstream-performance validation.

competitive_landscape.title: DiffusionNAG: Predictor-guided Neural Architecture Generation with Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior neural-architecture-generation method that already reframes NAS as generation
competitive_landscape.difference: DiffusionNAG conditionally generates architectures as directed graphs inside predefined NAS search spaces (including MobileNetV3), guided by parameterized performance predictors and validated by downstream accuracy and up-to-35x speedups; Younger contributes the data substrate for unrestricted-space generation but its own global-paradigm experiment is an unguided DiGress run reporting only NLL, so the claimed step beyond predictor-guided in-space generation is not yet empirically shown.

competitive_landscape.title: Multi-conditioned Graph Diffusion for Neural Architecture Search
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses discrete conditional graph diffusion with multi-conditioned classifier-free guidance (accuracy and hardware-latency constraints) and evaluates generated architectures on six benchmarks and ImageNet; Younger's diffusion experiment is unconditioned, restricted to <=300-node graphs, and never trains or scores a generated architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: DiGress: Discrete Denoising Diffusion for Graph Generation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Method dependency for the global paradigm
competitive_landscape.difference: DiGress is a general discrete graph-diffusion model developed and validated on molecular and small non-molecular graph benchmarks with validity/uniqueness metrics; Younger transplants it unchanged to operator DAGs an order of magnitude larger and reports only likelihood, so the transfer's adequacy for attributed, size-heterogeneous architecture DAGs is untested.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Zoos: A Dataset of Diverse Populations of Neural Network Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Complementary real-model dataset with the opposite design choice
competitive_landscape.difference: Model Zoos publishes 50,360 trained models (3.8M checkpoints) of small fixed architectures to study weight-space populations and generative modeling of parameters; Younger publishes parameter-free architecture topologies of diverse real models, so the two datasets partition the model artifact (weights vs structure) and neither alone supports performance-aware architecture generation.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v1 / NeurIPS 2022 Datasets and Benchmarks, 2022-09-29

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim Younger is the first dataset for AI-generated neural network architecture: the first large-scale, unrestricted (no predefined macro- or micro-architecture) collection of real-world operator-level architecture DAGs, enabling a new field (AIGNNA) with local and global design paradigms, and secondarily a novel GNN benchmark regime.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Table 1 positions Younger against NAS-Bench-101/201/NLP/ASR and DeepNets-1M on architecture restrictions, operator-type counts (193 ONNX vs 3-15 primitives), and task coverage (31 vs 1); Table 2 positions it against Cora/ZINC/QM9 on graph-count/size/node-type balance; Section 3 documents the 743.5K->7,629 pipeline.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The dataset claim largely holds: no prior public corpus offers deduplicated, operator-level, cross-framework DAGs of real deployed models at this scale, and DeepNets-1M (synthetic, image-only, 15 op types) is the nearest predecessor. The conceptual claim is weaker: reframing architecture search as generation predates this paper (DiffusionNAG and multi-conditioned graph diffusion already generate architectures with diffusion models, albeit inside fixed spaces), so AIGNNA is an extension of neural architecture generation to unrestricted spaces rather than a new field. The experimental support is the thinnest layer - near-saturated link prediction, long-tail-limited operator classification with inconsistent duplicate tables, and a single uninterpretable DiGress NLL - so Younger should be treated as a validated data resource with an unvalidated generation program, and the absence of performance labels is the decisive gap separating it from actionable NAS/NAG benchmarks.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass covered all 31 indexed pages, including the datasheet, maintenance/licensing appendices, experimental details (splits, hyperparameters, duplicate result tables), embedding visualizations, author contributions, and checklist. The indexed text reports 31/31 pages with text and no missing pages; provenance fields are copied verbatim from the fulltext index. The paper is a preprint marked 'Under review' with no venue or OpenReview record found. Author-reported numbers (Tables 3-5, 8, 11) were transcribed directly from the extracted text; the main-text/appendix discrepancies are flagged as a contradiction audit rather than resolved, since no code was executed in this pass. Competitive records were verified against live arXiv abstract pages on 2026-08-23 (NAS-Bench-101 v2, DeepNets-1M v1, DiffusionNAG v4, multi-conditioned graph diffusion v2, DiGress v4, Model Zoos v1). Confidence reflects a straightforward dataset paper with clearly stated construction and weak-but-transparent experiments; it is not higher because dataset statistics could not be independently recomputed and the duplicate-table inconsistency leaves exact metric values uncertain.
